newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Racism charges sully Austria local poll campaign.
newsitem.headline: Racism charges sully Austria local poll campaign.

text.p: Charges of racism forced a senior liberal candidate in Vienna municipal elections to withdraw on Monday, a week after the U.S. ambassador to Austria described far-right European election posters as "implicitly xenophobic".
Wolfgang Bachmayer, who topped the candidate list of the Liberal Forum party, quit in disgrace after it emerged he had made racist remarks at a far-right political seminar in 1992.

Bachmayer, 48, announced his withdrawal at a news conference after the weekly news magazine Profil reported his participation in a controversial 1992 seminar, organised by the far-right Freedom Party.
"I have become too much of a political burden for the party," the market researcher told reporters.
The Liberal Forum was set up by politicians who split from Joerg Haider's nationalist Freedom Party in February 1993, branding the far right as being too anti-foreigner.
Profil said in its Monday edition that Bachmayer told the 1992 meeting in the southern province of Carinthia that white babies begin to cry when confronted with a black face.
"However, a white baby reacts normally to a white face," Profil said, quoting from the minutes of the discussion.
Bachmayer initially defended his remarks as "scientifically correct", Profil said.
But on Sunday he conceded in an interview with Austrian radio that he may have spoken "without sufficient thought".
The Vienna state poll is scheduled for October 13, the same day as nationwide elections for the European Parliament.

The Austrian government issued a warning on Monday over new letter bomb attacks in the run-up to the elections. The Interior Ministry said it was necessary to remind Austrians to beware of suspect packages over the next two weeks.

Austria has been hit by a series of bombings since December 1993, many coinciding with local or nationwide polls. Four gypsies were killed in a booby-trapped bomb last year and around a dozen people have been injured in letter bomb blasts.
Police suspect right-wing extremists as most victims have been foreigners or figures sympathetic to immigrant issues.

The racism row broke out a week after the mayor of Chicago, Richard Daley, hit out at the choice of slogan chosen by the Freedom Party in its European election campaign -- "Vienna must not become like Chicago".

In a letter to Daley, Vienna far-right leader Rainer Pawkowicz said he had not intended to imply a failure in Daley's policies but the inability of the Social Democrat-run city hall in tackling rising crime in the Austrian capital.

U.S. ambassador to Austria, Swanee Hunt, wrote to the far-right party, objecting to what she described as "the attempted portrayal of an American city as a negative 'role model' and to the implicit xenophobia of the posters".
The U.S. embassy said it was disappointed the posters had not been removed as promised by the Freedom Party. Many could still be seen around Vienna city centre on Monday.
While the far right is expected to improve on its 22 percent showing in last December's general election, the Liberal Forum could be damaged by Bachmayer's withdrawal.
"Bachmayer's comments have made the Liberal Forum less convincing -- and not only in Vienna," party leader Heide Schmidt told reporters.
